newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW - Telecom NZ reviews Pacific Star.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Telecom NZ reviews Pacific Star.

text.p: Telecom Corp of New Zealand Ltd has confirmed it is continuing to review whether it should sell its Australian bridgehead, Pacific Star Group.
"Pacific Star has been a bridgehead for us...but now it's under review, which is a natural evolution over three years," Telecom chairman Peter Shirtcliffe told Reuters in a recent interview.
Telecom NZ has previously said it may sell some or all of Pacific Star.

In reporting a first quarter net profit of NZ$177.1 million last month, Telecom said Pacific Star had made an overall loss for the period, reflecting planned start-up activities and also highly competitive conditions in the Australian market.
Telecom did give details of the loss incurred by Pacific Star.
Shirtcliffe would not give any details about when or if Pacific Star might be sold.

Telecom's general manager of business development and chairman of Pacific Star, John Bell, said in August that Pacific Star had been developed initially as a discount broker and value-added service provider.
It had grown to be a significant-sized unit with a strategic position in the Australian market.

However, recent developments in the Australian environment, together with pricing policy changes on the part of Pacific Star's principal supplier Telstra, meant that Pacific Star may no longer be the perfect fit for Telecom.
"It is possible that, in the changing Australasian environment, some or indeed all of Pacific Star could be worth more to another operator than to us," Bell said then.
Analysts have said Telecom is eyeing a much more substantial role in the Australian telecommunications scene after the July 1, 1997 deregulation.
This may involve a full-scale alliance with either Telstra or Optus, rather than a stand-alone operation competing with the two dominant Australian operators.
Shirtcliffe said Telecom wanted to be a substantial long-term stakeholder in the Australian market, which he saw as eventually merging with the New Zealand market under a single set of rules.
Telecom NZ, which is owned 24.8 percent owned by Bell Atlantic Corp and 24.8 percent owned by Ameritech Corp, also has another smaller bridgehead in Australia.
Telecom said in April it had bought Brisbane-based DVP, an interactive digital media company specialising in new media applications, for an undisclosed sum.
DVP uses digital technology to combine sound, pictures and data to create interactive media for business clients in a range of industries.
DVP was founded in 1993 and employs 40 people.
Telecom said there were plans to grow the business to over 200 people over the next five years.
